newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end off on renewed inflation jitters.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end off on renewed inflation jitters.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed lower on Thursday after renewed inflation jitters spooked players and sent prices down sharply for the fourth straight session.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark bond ended down 22/32 at 98-9/32. Its yield jumped to 6.89 percent, above the 6.88 percent seen prior to the issue of the September payroll data.

Pundits said bearish comments by a top Federal Reserve official combined with a surprising drop in jobless claims re-ignited inflation jitters and cast a shadow on some economists' steady monetary policy view.

Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer suggested in an interview with the Investors Business Daily that a slowdown in economic activity might not be enough to prevent a pick up in inflation if wages continued to climb.
"The question is -- and I don't think we can run away from that -- 'Is the unemployment rate already so low that if it stays there inflation will rise in the future?" Meyer was quoted as saying.
The comments added to some bearish remarks by Fed governor Lawrence Lindsey on Wednesday, when he said that curbing inflation may mean a temporary rise in future interest rates.

"The scenario appears to be getting a little bleaker. It really looks like Fed officials decided to come out and say they are concerned about tight labor markets and inflation," said a trader at a major U.S. investment bank.

Analysts also said a second look at the latest employment report, which showed non-farm payrolls dropped by 40,000 in September, appears to indicate the numbers were more likely to be a blip rather than a trend.
"The market thought a little bit more about the employment report and decided that it might not be consistent with reality," said Paul Kasriel, economist at Northern Trust Co.

Pundits said the release on Thursday of a surprising drop to 319,000 in jobless claims in the week ended October 5 from a revised 341,000 in the previous seven-day period suggested the labor market remained very tight.

"We got some evidence to support the idea that the payroll report was not consistent with reality even with today's jobless claims," Kasriel said. "People are getting a little nervous about the inflation outlook."
Although everyone agrees it remains a very close call, some scaterred analysts in the market are reconsidering the possibility of a Fed interest rate hike in November.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the central bank's policy-setting arm, is scheduled to meet next on November 13. It will then meet again on December 17.

"My best guess right now would be a 25 basis point (hike) on November 13 and another 25 basis points at the December (FOMC) meeting," said Waldo Best, senior economist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd Government Inc.
Analysts said a 0.4 percent rise in the Chicago Fed manufacturing index to 129.4 in August versus a revised 129.0 in July was seen as bearish to the market as well.

Analysts said a large amount of new corporate issues, combined with the market's hangover from Tuesday's 10-year note auction and Thrusday's sale of $19.3 billion of 52-week bills, also weighed heavily on prices.
The Treasury placed the year bills at 5.34 percent.
Pundits said the market's eyes are now all focused on the release on Friday of the producer price index (PPI) and the retail sales report. Both for the month of September.
Some analysts said prices have dropped so sharply in anticipation to the data that a relief rally has not been discounted.
"We might be marching up for a little of bounce tomorrow. It's getting overdone a little bit here...It could a classic case of selling the rumor and buying the fact," Best said.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed up three basis points at 5.02 percent. The six-month bill rate rose five points to 5.15 percent. The year bill rate was up six points at 5.31 percent.

The two-year note closed down 3/32 at 100-0/32, yielding 6.00 percent. The five-year note traded off 8/32 at 100-1/32 to yield 6.37 percent. The ten-year note closed down 14/32 at 99-6/32, yielding 6.61 percent. -- 212-859-1676
